page: Amazon Web Services c5a.4xlarge is a compute-optimized instance built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor architecture. It features a 64-bit AMD EPYC 7R32 processor running at 3.3 GHz, offering 16 vCPUs across 8 physical cores with 2 threads per core. The instance is configured with 32.0 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, maintaining a 1:2 compute-to-memory ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU. It does not include dedicated graphics processing units, local instance storage, or complimentary public IPv4 addresses, requiring remote network storage solutions for persistent data. Baseline network bandwidth is provisioned at 5 Gbps.

Benchmark results demonstrate reliable multi-core throughput alongside modest single-thread metrics. In stress-ng evaluations, the server achieves a multi-core score of 6142.7, aligning with mid-tier industry expectations, while its single-core score of 767.39 sits in the lower performance brackets. Geekbench metrics reinforce this profile, delivering a multi-core score of 7998.0 and a single-core score of 1339.0. Memory throughput reveals substantial variation depending on cache levels; cached read bandwidth reaches 800.68 GB/sec, whereas uncached large-block transfers decline to 37.14 GB/sec for reads and 22.42 GB/sec for writes.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the c5a series utilizes AMD EPYC architecture to supply dedicated compute capacity at a lower hardware overhead than comparable alternatives. The absence of built-in NVMe storage lowers base operational expenditure for stateless systems, though network storage I/O must be accounted for in overall design. Workloads such as Clang software compilation, multi-threaded compression algorithms, static web serving, and distributed batch processing align effectively with its multi-core capabilities and 5 Gbps networking.

This server type is primarily recommended for parallelized computation tasks that operate within moderate RAM constraints. Typical applications include CI/CD build environments, web server farms handling static or lightly stateful requests, background processing queues, and microservices architectures that do not require GPU acceleration or large resident database datasets.
